Individuals with HIV or other medical conditions that compromise immunity, as well as those taking medications like anti-TNF agents or steroids that suppress immune function, are at increased risk and require careful monitoring. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) now recommends tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) regimens that shorten the treatment duration to three months or less. However, active tuberculosis (TB) disease still requires a minimum of six months of treatment, starting with a combination of four medications. 3. Healthcare providers should inform patients about the potential risks associated with TPT and the likelihood of adverse events occurring. 4. Patients undergoing TPT should be aware that red discoloration of urine and other bodily fluids is a harmless and normal side effect of rifamycin therapy when using regimens such as 3HR, 3HP, 1HP, or 4R. 5. Common adverse drug reactions during TPT include gastrointestinal disturbances, flu-like symptoms, liver injury (hepatotoxicity), and skin rashes. 6. Patients should be educated to recognize early signs of hepatotoxicity, such as weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, and persistent nausea. Early detection of hepatotoxicity is crucial, as it is reversible and does not lead to permanent damage if addressed promptly. 7. Late signs of hepatotoxicity include liver tenderness, liver enlargement (hepatomegaly), and jaundice. Patients should also be vigilant for flu-like symptoms or acute reactions shortly after taking rifapentine-containing TPT, which may occur most commonly after the third dose. 8. If any of the above symptoms or changes in health status occur, patients should immediately contact their healthcare provider for advice and continue treatment only if advised to do so. 9. Patients should understand that TB disease can still develop during TPT. While symptom screening is typically conducted before starting TPT to rule out active TB, patients should remain alert for symptoms such as cough, unexplained weight loss, fever, and night sweats. If these symptoms arise, they should notify their provider and undergo testing for TB disease. 10. In young children, non-specific signs such as failure to thrive, reduced playfulness, and decreased appetite should be closely monitored, as they may indicate early TB disease. 11. Women of childbearing age should be counseled to use barrier methods of contraception while on TPT, as pregnancy can occur during treatment. Safety data on the use of rifapentine-containing regimens during pregnancy is limited. 12. If pregnancy occurs during 3HP or 1HP regimens, it is recommended to switch to a six-month daily isoniazid regimen. Pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV may use a fixed-dose combination of isoniazid, cotrimoxazole, and vitamin B6, along with supportive care and monitoring. 13. Adherence to TPT is influenced by various factors, including clinic hours, competing priorities (e.g., work, school, caregiving), long wait times, costs associated with clinic visits, and insufficient information about TB infection, treatment regimens, and disease. 14. Stigma related to TB infection, disease, and treatment, as well as personal health beliefs and practices, can also act as barriers to adherence. Some individuals may perceive TPT as more of a burden than a benefit. 15. Treatment-related issues, such as coexisting medical conditions, concurrent use of other medications or supplements, adverse drug reactions, alcohol intake, difficulty remembering doses, and religious practices like fasting, can further complicate adherence. 16. Strategies to improve adherence include exploring the patient’s understanding of TB and TPT, involving family members or treatment buddies for support, and emphasizing the importance of taking medication at a consistent time. 17. Patients should be encouraged to complete the full course of treatment for optimal protection against TB. They should also be advised to report any adverse drug reactions, even mild ones, to their provider. 18. Medications should be taken together as a single dose rather than divided over several hours or days. If necessary, pills can be separated but should be consumed within 30 minutes. 19. Reminders, such as electronic alerts on cell phones or aligning medication schedules with daily routines or religious practices, can help patients take their medication regularly. 20. Healthcare providers should align TPT delivery and follow-up with other services the patient is receiving, such as TB or HIV care, and provide motivational counseling through trained providers. 21. Identifying a treatment supporter, such as a family member, neighbor, or colleague, can help ensure adherence. Providers should maintain confidentiality while recording contact information for the patient and their close contacts. 22. In-person encounters should be scheduled for individuals who frequently miss appointments or whose treatment has been interrupted. Digital adherence technologies, such as electronic pillboxes with SIM cards or video-supported therapy, may also be used when in-person visits are not feasible. 23. Incentives, such as grocery store coupons or food parcels, may encourage adherence, though their effectiveness in improving adherence is not well-established. 24. Enablers, such as reimbursement for transportation costs or phone calls, can make it easier for patients to keep appointments, depending on the availability of resources and staff. 25. An adherence plan should be developed with the patient and reviewed at each visit. This plan may include motivators for staying TB-free, strategies for taking medication with food to reduce nausea, and actions to take in case of vomiting after medication. 26. For children, barriers to adherence include the lack of child-friendly medication formulations, caregiver skepticism about the importance of TPT, and family factors such as the absence of a consistent caregiver or changes in routine. 27. Strategies to enhance adherence in children include explaining the importance of completing the full course of treatment, providing clear instructions on dissolving dispersible formulations, and offering a person-friendly schedule for drug refills. 28. Caregivers should be educated about early signs of hepatotoxicity in children and how to manage vomiting after medication, including providing extra doses if necessary. 29. Adolescents should receive direct education and adherence support, especially if they are living with HIV. 30. For young children refusing medication, alternative strategies include masking the taste of crushed pills with different foods, placing the medication in the center of solid food, or offering a treat as a reward for taking the medication. 31. Healthcare providers should reassure patients that they can return at any time if they miss a dose or face challenges in continuing their medication. 32. Scheduled follow-ups should occur at intervals appropriate to the country context (e.g., fortnightly, monthly, quarterly) and may take place in clinics, communities, or households. These encounters provide opportunities to assess adherence, address barriers, and update records. 33. Providers should use motivational interviewing techniques to improve adherence, check for adverse events and TB symptoms, and verify contact information to ensure effective communication.
